entities.summary:
Antarctica's discovery in the early 19th century marked a pivotal moment in human exploration and scientific inquiry. The continent, long shrouded in mystery, was finally mapped by Edward Bransfield in 1820, and its icy landscape has since been the subject of numerous expeditions and research stations.

 As the world's most inhospitable environment, Antarctica has played a significant role in shaping our understanding of climate change, astronomy, and the natural sciences. The Antarctic Treaty System, established in 1959, has protected the continent from military occupation and environmental degradation, setting a precedent for international cooperation on the global stage.

 Despite its remote location, Antarctica has left an indelible mark on human history, inspiring countless scientists, explorers, and artists to pursue their passions. From Sir Ernest Shackleton's ill-fated Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition to the modern-day research stations that dot the landscape, Antarctica continues to captivate our imagination and inspire our sense of wonder.

 "The most important single element in achieving world peace is the secure and reliable supply of energy." - Robert McNamara

Their legacy is studied through the lens of historical causation.", "summary": "Antarctica is the world's fifth-largest continent — 14.2 million km² of land (98% covered by ice averaging 2.1 km deep), containing 70% of the world's fresh water in frozen form. The coldest, driest, and windiest continent on Earth, it is the only continent without a permanent human population and without any indigenous human history: no Homo sapiens ever reached Antarctica before the early 19th century, and the last continent to be discovered (the first confirmed sighting was in 1820). The Antarctic ice sheet, if fully melted, would raise global sea levels by approximately 60 metres — making it the most consequential ice mass for the future of human civilisation in a warming world.

Antarctica's human history begins with the 'Heroic Age' of polar exploration (1897–1922): the Belgian Belgica expedition (1897), the British Discovery expedition under Robert Falcon Scott (1901–1904), Ernest Shackleton's Nimrod expedition (1907–1909) and his legendary Endurance voyage (1914–1917), and Roald Amundsen's Norwegian team reaching the South Pole on 14 December 1911 — thirty-four days before Scott's team, which perished on the return journey. The race to the South Pole was one of the defining episodes of early 20th-century nationalism and heroism, and Shackleton's Endurance survival — his entire crew of 28 rescued without a single fatality after 634 days stranded — remains the greatest survival story in exploration history.

The Antarctic Treaty System (1959, in force 1961) is one of the most successful international agreements in history: 54 nations have signed, and the treaty designates Antarctica as a scientific preserve, bans military activity and mineral extraction, and suspends all territorial claims for the treaty's duration.
